title: How Good Leaders Localize the ‘Why’ After Announcing Major Change r-change/
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: The piece refines a move most change-management writing gets half right. Every change-leadership framework insists on communicating the why, and Admired Leadership grants the point: people want the rationale behind a decision so they can align their own work to the outcome. But the authors argue there is a second question that matters even more to each individual team member, even the most selfless, and most leaders underinvest in answering it. The question is: how will this affect me? The logic is straightforward and too often ignored. Organizational change already carries uncertainty. When the leader announces a direction without translating what the change means for a specific person's daily work, scope, job security, required skills, or workload, the uncertainty curdles into threat. People react sharply because the global ‘why’ does not resolve the local ‘what now.’ Leaders who skip this localization invite ridicule, resistance, and reaction, and pay for the shortcut with slower adoption and erosion of trust. The prescription is operational. The leader must consider the ramifications of the change for each team member and then actually communicate what they see or anticipate. Those whose work will change dramatically should be told immediately; delay corrodes trust faster than hard news does. The conversations should be planned and sequenced, not left to happen organically, which is why a real rollout is a coordinated process rather than a single announcement. Telling people what they most want to learn, quickly and specifically, is how full subscription to the change is actually built.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: When leaders and organizations make changes, everyone wants to know why. The rationale or reason behind any decision or change allows people to grasp the bigger picture and predict how their tasks and actions must align to achieve the desired outcome.

People’s desire to learn and understand the “Why” is natural and intense. The “Why” gives meaning and purpose to action. Without it, team members are left to follow blindly without a pathway to avoid or correct mistakes.

But as important as the “Why” is, there is a second question regarding change that is even more important to each and every team member, no matter how selfless they may be. They want to know the answer to one very important question: How will this affect me?

Leaders who answer the “Why” without localizing what it means at the individual level miss an important lever for buy-in and quality execution. Narrowing down the impact of the change on individual performance is required for full subscription and engagement.
The uncertainty of organizational change is hard enough to deal with. But coupled with not knowing how the change will impact them and their work makes the change threatening.
Leaders who fail to localize the impact or effect of the change on each and every team member invite ridicule, resistance, and reaction.

For those whose work lives will change dramatically as a result of the change, telling them immediately prevents an erosion of trust that can spread like wildfire inside the organization. As difficult as these conversations might be, keeping people in the dark has far greater and more negative consequences.
Presuming they will happen on their own is folly and a recipe for dissent. That’s why “rolling out” a major change is a strategic process.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
